about.title: Hidden Hills Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Hidden Hills is a small, gated equestrian community in Los Angeles County, and much of the work done here happens on private residential estates, ranch properties, and small commercial sites rather than in large industrial settings. That means workplace injuries in Hidden Hills often involve landscaping crews, equestrian staff, contractors, delivery drivers, or maintenance workers hurt on someone else's property. California generally requires injured workers to go through workers' compensation, but when a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or another driver contributed to the accident, a separate third-party claim may be possible alongside your comp benefits. LawProactive is a free service — not a law firm — that connects injured workers with an independent attorney who can look at the details of your accident, explain your rights, and help you figure out whether more than one avenue applies. Attorneys in our network work on contingency, so there's no upfront cost to find out where you stand.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About Your Workplace Injury

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Story
items.desc: California workers' compensation is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party — like a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment maker — may still owe you a separate claim.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Move Fast
items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, and missing that window can complicate your comp benefits.

items.title: Retaliation Is Illegal, But Workers Still Worry
items.desc: California law prohibits employers from punishing you for reporting an injury or filing a claim, and an attorney can help if you feel pressured to stay quiet.

items.question: I was hurt working on a private estate in Hidden Hills — does workers' comp still apply?
items.answer: In most cases, yes — California workers' compensation applies regardless of fault, even for work done on private residential or ranch properties. But if a property owner, contractor, or equipment supplier was negligent, you may also have a separate third-party claim worth exploring. An independent attorney can review the specifics of your situation.

items.question: What if my employer says I can't file a claim because I'm a contractor?
items.answer: Whether you're classified as an employee or independent contractor affects your options, and misclassification disputes are common. This is exactly the kind of question an attorney should look at closely before you accept what you're told.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a third-party injury claim in California?
items.answer: Third-party claims connected to a workplace injury generally carry a two-year deadline from the date of the accident. Workers' comp reporting requirements are separate and move faster, so it helps to get guidance early rather than waiting.

items.question: Does LawProactive charge anything to connect me with an attorney?
items.answer: No. LawProactive is a free service, and attorneys in our network work on contingency, meaning there's no fee unless you recover compensation.
